The incubation period of the Great shearwater (Ardenna gravis) has been documented in field studies on Nightingale Island, where eggs maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] require approximately 53 days [ab = approximately 53 days] to hatch. This relatively extended incubation period, compared to smaller procellariiforms, reflects the substantial energetic investment required to develop a large, yolk-dependent embryo within a calcareous egg. Upon hatching, the altricial downy chick emerges at a wet weight of 230 grams [Wwb = 230 grams], a neonatal mass that represents a modest fraction of the ultimate adult size. The nestling phase is characterized by rapid mass gain, with the chick attaining an asymptotic mass prior to fledging of 1300 grams [Wwi = 1300 grams], markedly exceeding the mean adult body mass of approximately 860 grams. This overshoot in body mass is a common strategy among burrow-nesting seabirds, providing lipid reserves that buffer the fledgling against the energetic demands of its first post-fledging dispersal and the initial period of nutritional independence.

Under the basal thermal conditions associated with active adult metabolism, measured at 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental milestones governs the early life history of this pelagic procellariid. The fledgling typically achieves its first flight and departs the nesting burrow at 108 days after hatching [tx = 108 days after hatching], a stage marked by the completion of flight feather maturation and the onset of post-fledging dispersal at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This timing aligns with the general pattern observed in other burrow-nesting procellariids of similar body size. Following nest departure, the immature bird undergoes a prolonged period of somatic growth and learning at sea before reaching the physiological state of puberty. Field data from banding studies indicate that the onset of gonadal maturation, or puberty, occurs at 324 days after hatching [tp = 324 days after hatching], coinciding with the end of the first year of life at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This timing suggests that young Great shearwaters attain sexual maturity relatively rapidly compared to some other long-lived seabirds of the Southern Ocean, many of which delay puberty until their second or third year.

Life-history theory predicts that long-lived seabirds delay their first breeding attempt until several years after reaching sexual maturity, a pattern that has been confirmed for the Great shearwater through long-term resighting studies at the colony. The age at first successful reproduction, meaning the production of the first brood, has been estimated at 5 years after hatching [tR = 5 years after hatching], a delay that aligns with the values reported for the closely related Manx shearwater (Puffinus puffinus) at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This extended pre-breeding period is interpreted as a bet-hedging strategy, allowing the young adult to accumulate sufficient foraging experience and body condition to sustain the considerable energetic costs of a single-egg clutch. Under the same thermal conditions of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], the potential maximum reproductive rate of the species is constrained by this life-history schedule and the protracted period required to rear a single chick to independence.

The maximum lifespan of the Great shearwater has been inferred from data for the closely related Manx shearwater, which indicates a longevity of approximately 50.9 years [am = approximately 50.9 years] at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This extreme lifespan, characteristic of many procellariiforms, is supported by the species' low annual mortality rates among breeding adults and its capacity to defer reproduction over many years. Records of banded individuals from the South Atlantic suggest that Great shearwaters may achieve comparable longevity, although direct estimates for the species remain limited by the duration of marking programs. The low overall reproductive rate, with a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and typically one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year], is offset by a high probability of adult survival across decades, a classic demographic trade-off among pelagic seabirds. This combination of slow reproduction and extended lifespan favors the evolution of high parental investment per offspring, as observed in the extended incubation and brooding periods documented earlier.

Seasonal migrations of the Great shearwater between breeding colonies in the Tristan da Cunha archipelago and non-breeding foraging grounds in the North Atlantic impose substantial physiological demands on the population. During the breeding season, the adults alternate between incubation bouts at the burrow and long-distance foraging trips that can extend for several days across the South Atlantic. The rapid growth of the nestling, sustained by regurgitated meals of fish, squid, and crustaceans provided by both parents, is tightly synchronized with the seasonal peak in local marine productivity, ensuring adequate food availability for provisioning adults. This tight coupling between the species' phenology and the oceanic environment underscores the vulnerability of Great shearwater populations to climate-driven shifts in prey distribution and sea surface temperatures.
